analysis.one_liner: Requires states to pay welfare benefits to poor families of at least half the poverty line.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; it got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan proposed requiring every state's Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program to pay benefits that, when combined with food stamps, reach at least 50 percent of the federal poverty line for a family's size. This would have raised cash welfare payments in many states, where benefits fell well below that level. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Very low-income families with children receiving AFDC, particularly in states with low benefit levels, who would have seen cash payments and food stamp benefits rise toward half the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state's AFDC plan to set payment standards so that cash aid plus the family's food stamp allotment equals or exceeds 50 percent of the federal poverty line for the family's size [S2] [S3].
Sets a floor across states, so benefits could no longer be dramatically lower in some states than others for the same-sized family [S3].
Gave states time to comply: the standard took effect October 1, 1992, with an additional delay for states needing legislation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments, which share AFDC costs with the federal government, would have had to raise their benefit standards, and federal costs would also rise where the minimum bound.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no dedicated federal funding stream, so the cost of raising benefits to the 50-percent floor would have fallen substantially on state budgets, which some would object to as an unfunded mandate [S3].
Opponents of higher welfare benefits argued that richer payments could increase program rolls and reduce incentives to work, a standard objection to raising AFDC payment floors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have raised a meaningful income floor for the poorest families with children, but it left the financing question open, making states the likely bearers of most of the cost. The failure of even a single senator to cosponsor it suggests the funding design did not attract support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Moynihan introduced the Minimum Benefit for Families Act of 1991 on April 17, 1991 [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no cosponsors joined [S4], and the bill died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that would have had to raise welfare payments to meet a 50-percent poverty floor are better off that the bill died. Families on AFDC in low-benefit states gained nothing; benefits stayed where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States that would have paid more

for.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-NY), bill sponsor and member of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to his own committee, the Senate Finance Committee; it drew no other Senate support.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a hearing or markup; the bill received no committee action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no roll calls exist; the only recorded facts are that Moynihan sponsored it alone with zero cosponsors from either party and that his own party's committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required states to raise their welfare payment standards toward half the poverty line, a cost states would largely bear through their share of AFDC funding. States with the lowest benefits had the strongest interest in blocking such a floor, since their interest in keeping payments low ran directly against the income floor poor families needed.
